title: Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that durably clears an established, mature bacterial biofilm while preserving a stable, useful orthopedic reconstruction, without indefinite antibiotic suppression. In an infected joint replacement or fixation construct, this would mean eliminating the infection while retaining the functioning reconstruction. The central advance is durable clearance after a finite course of treatment, rather than control that depends on continued antimicrobial therapy.

Biofilm is a community of bacteria attached to a surface. In implant-associated infection, bacteria within mature biofilm can tolerate antibiotics even when conventional susceptibility tests suggest that those drugs should work. Antibiotic-tolerant persister cells help explain why infection can relapse after treatment stops. Rottier, Seidelman, and Wouthuyzen-Bakker’s review, published on 2 March 2023, describes why chronic implant-associated infection often requires foreign-body removal for source control and why debridement plus systemic antimicrobials alone cannot be assumed to eradicate mature biofilm.

A proposed extension is to eradicate infection in chronic osteomyelitis while preserving structurally important bone, including cases involving a sequestrum, or separated dead bone. This remains part of the concept’s intended scope, but the supplied evidence primarily concerns periprosthetic joint infection and does not establish the sequestrum-specific biological rationale or demonstrate successful bone preservation. Retained bone would need to remain mechanically useful; eliminating bacteria would not itself restore dead bone to living tissue.

significance.text: A reliable cure with reconstruction retention would change the surgical consequences of chronic orthopedic infection. Eligible patients could keep an already functioning joint replacement or fixation construct and avoid infection-driven removal and replacement, including some two-stage revisions. Avoiding those operations could also reduce the bone sacrificed during removal and reconstruction. The revolutionary capability would be dependable treatment of mature infection while preserving useful structure.

Conditional impact assessment: fewer amputations after failed limb salvage would be a possible downstream benefit, rather than an assured direct consequence. Limb preservation also depends on tissue viability, blood supply, soft-tissue coverage and mechanical stability. Infection clearance alone would not repair damaged soft tissue, restore dead bone or make an unstable reconstruction functional. These constraints would determine which patients could benefit from retention.

This advance would address infection-related loss of a reconstruction, not lifelong freedom from aseptic loosening or particle-related osteolysis. Many hip replacements already last decades: Whitehouse and colleagues’ PLOS Medicine analysis, published on 7 November 2024 and involving 1,026,481 National Joint Registry hip replacements, cites earlier evidence that 58% to 78% of total hip replacements last more than 25 years. That range is contextual prior evidence, not a newly demonstrated 25-year result from the million-hip cohort. Long implant survival and the ability to cure established infection remain distinct achievements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reproducible elimination of mature biofilm from a retained reconstruction, with durable infection control after finite therapy. The biological obstacle includes organisms that remain antibiotic tolerant despite conventional susceptibility, particularly persister populations capable of contributing to relapse. A treatment must address the established infection sufficiently to replace the source-control benefit ordinarily obtained by removing infected foreign material; temporary symptom improvement or reduced bacterial burden would not establish that capability.

Engineering synthesis: a successful approach would need to reach infected surfaces and surrounding reservoirs, maintain effective activity throughout the treated region, and preserve the implant, bone and soft tissue needed for function. It would also need to work within defined organism and clinical boundaries, rather than relying on susceptibility results alone. Antimicrobial drugs, local delivery systems and biofilm-directed technologies could contribute, but the supplied evidence does not identify a particular platform as having solved this combined problem.

The bone-preservation extension adds a separate challenge: deciding what infected bone can remain useful and demonstrating both durable infection control and retained structural function. Sterilization and viability are different endpoints. The supplied materials leave unresolved whether, and under what conditions, sequestrum-containing bone could be preserved successfully instead of excised.

current_state.text: Existing treatment already includes debridement, antibiotics and implant retention, commonly abbreviated DAIR, for selected early infections associated with immature biofilm. Biofilm-active antimicrobial treatment also exists: the 2023 review discusses rifampicin combinations for staphylococcal infection, fluoroquinolones for selected Gram-negative infections, and fluoroquinolones as companion drugs in some rifampicin regimens. Their usefulness depends on the organism and clinical context. These treatments accompany surgical source control; their existence does not establish dependable eradication of chronic mature biofilm with the entire reconstruction preserved.

An umbrella review by Lu, Zhang, and Xia was accepted on 21 September 2026 and published online on 28 October 2026 as an Article in Press in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. It reports pooled DAIR failure of 35.9%, rising to 73.6% in late chronic cases. It also reports descriptive mortality of 11.0% after hip periprosthetic joint infection and 13.3% after knee infection. Table 2 rates these burden estimates as having very low certainty. Definitions and follow-up periods varied, so these percentages should not be treated as directly comparable risks, causal treatment effects or measurements of microbiological sterilization.

Partial preservation during revision is an important existing achievement. The same umbrella review reports pooled infection eradication of 88% and implant stability of 89% for chronic total hip arthroplasty infection treated by partial two-stage revision while retaining a stable femoral component. This qualifies any assertion that chronic infection always requires removal of every component. It represents selective component retention during reconstruction-changing surgery, rather than demonstration of reliable clearance while preserving the entire functioning reconstruction.

The supplied review had complete main-article text for the 2023 treatment review and the 2026 umbrella review. The umbrella review’s retained HTML contained only the abstract and metadata, but its complete 25-page main article supported the numerical findings and certainty qualifications. Supplementary materials and figure images were not inspected. Its literature search ended on 20 April 2026, and no additional bounded freshness search was supplied. The evidence therefore documents persistent difficulty treating mature biofilm without establishing that every reconstruction-preserving clinical method is ineffective or that no qualifying advance existed on 1 November 2026.

The earlier research also asserted that experimental local delivery can reduce bacterial counts in animals followed by rebound. The supplied evidence review did not substantiate that specific result, so it cannot be presented here as a demonstrated finding. This evidentiary gap does not establish that the assertion is false. Likewise, the materials do not provide a clinical dataset demonstrating the proposed sequestrum-preserving extension.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospectively evaluate patients with chronic periprosthetic joint infection while retaining a stable, functioning reconstruction. Preregister durable infection control at two years after completion of finite antimicrobial therapy, without indefinite antibiotic suppression. Follow-up after treatment withdrawal matters because biofilm-associated infection can relapse after therapy stops. The 2023 review describes a clinical precedent for assessing persistence or relapse within two years after antibiotic withdrawal; this supports the proposed follow-up interval without making it an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Two-year infection control after finite therapy with functioning reconstruction retained

completion_criteria.text: Proposed endpoint design: specify microbiological sampling sites, timing and culture methods, alongside a preregistered clinical definition of infection control. Assess recurrence involving the original organism and define how new infection, additional surgery, amputation and death enter the analysis. Negative cultures should support the conclusion but should not be treated as proof that every organism has been eliminated. Document retained mechanical function and treatment harms as well as infection outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered endpoints define infection control and comprehensive treatment outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparative ambition: match an explicitly defined aseptic-revision benchmark for the same joint. This requires a genuinely comparable endpoint, adjustment for relevant patient differences and a prespecified statistical margin; aseptic revision outcomes cannot simply be equated with infection eradication. The benchmark and two-year threshold are proposed criteria for this concept, not published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Match comparable same-joint aseptic-revision outcomes within a prespecified statistical margin

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: obtain independent, preferably multicenter confirmation and report results by organism, chronicity, implant type, prior treatment and relevant patient characteristics. Separately test chronic osteomyelitis with sequestrum, documenting which bone is preserved, its viability or incorporation, and its mechanical usefulness. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within these tested settings, not literal universality. Individual phage-therapy case reports, prevention-only coatings and partial component retention alone would not establish the full proposed capability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent confirmation establishes scope across implants and chronic osteomyelitis

related_concepts.text: Within the supplied roster, ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, addresses rebuilding a lost limb, whereas ORT-03 aims to preserve an existing reconstruction threatened by infection. ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, could address a bone defect remaining after infection treatment. ORT-03 instead seeks to avoid infection-driven removal of useful structure where feasible. These capabilities could complement one another, but infection clearance does not itself regenerate a limb or replace a segmental bone defect.

ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, concerns restoration of a diseased native joint. ORT-03 concerns eradication of infection in bone or an orthopedic reconstruction, including an artificial joint. ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis, and ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, likewise target tissue-specific restoration. Infection control could enable such repairs in infected settings, but would not demonstrate restoration of their specialized anatomy or load-bearing function.

ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss, and ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps, address functional deficits that may coexist with complex limb infection. Successful ORT-03 treatment could preserve a setting in which those repairs remain possible, but would not restore missing muscle force or nerve conduction. Their separate contributions also explain why infection clearance alone cannot guarantee successful limb salvage.

ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, concerns controlling where and how bone forms. ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate, concerns restoration of organized longitudinal growth. Neither capability is supplied by bacterial eradication. They could become relevant when preserved or reconstructed bone needs further biological repair, while remaining distinct innovations.

Beyond the roster, ORT-03 overlaps with antimicrobial development, biofilm biology, phage approaches and local delivery technologies. Preventive coatings address initial contamination or adhesion; selected acute-infection retention protocols address a different disease stage; partial revision retains selected components; and implant-longevity research addresses durability beyond infection. These adjacent capabilities help define the target but do not individually demonstrate durable mature-biofilm clearance with preservation of the functioning reconstruction.

change_log.change: Preserved ORT-03’s identity, title and bone-preservation ambition while distinguishing the documented implant-associated problem from the proposed sequestrum extension.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports the central mature-biofilm rationale but does not establish sequestrum-specific biology or successful preservation.

change_log.change: Corrected the umbrella review’s acceptance date to 21 September 2026 and publication date to 28 October 2026; retained its Article in Press designation.
change_log.reason: The earlier text confused publication with acceptance.

change_log.change: Retained the DAIR failure and mortality estimates, adding very low certainty, variable follow-up and limits on comparison and interpretation.
change_log.reason: The numerical findings are supported, but they do not directly measure sterilization or establish causal comparative effectiveness.

change_log.change: Added the reported 88% eradication and 89% stability outcomes for partial two-stage hip revision retaining a stable femoral component.
change_log.reason: Existing selective component retention qualifies blanket claims about mandatory complete implant removal while remaining distinct from whole-reconstruction preservation.

change_log.change: Specified organism-dependent roles for rifampicin combinations and fluoroquinolones alongside surgical source control.
change_log.reason: The earlier phrasing obscured the clinical and microbiological boundaries of biofilm-active treatment.

change_log.change: Replaced the categorical absence claim with a bounded account of what the supplied evidence establishes and identified the animal-rebound assertion as unsubstantiated here.
change_log.reason: The freshness record is empty, the umbrella review searched through April 2026, and no supplied passage supports the animal result.

change_log.change: Separated direct reconstruction-preservation benefits from conditional reductions in amputation and added viability and mechanical limits.
change_log.reason: Infection eradication alone cannot resolve every cause of failed limb salvage.

change_log.change: Corrected attribution of the hip-longevity context to Whitehouse and colleagues and identified the 25-year range as cited prior evidence.
change_log.reason: The supplied review establishes the byline and shows that the range was not newly demonstrated by the million-hip cohort.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria with post-treatment follow-up, interpretable microbiology, competing outcomes, comparator definition, independent replication and a separate bone-preservation demonstration.
change_log.reason: These refinements make the proposed test meaningful without treating negative cultures as proof of sterilization or proposed thresholds as consensus standards.

change_log.change: Explained distinctions and potential complementarity across all other supplied roster entries.
change_log.reason: The infection-eradication capability remains separate from tissue regeneration, growth control and functional repair.

unresolved_issues: Sequestrum-specific evidence is still needed to establish when infected bone can be preserved with durable infection control and useful mechanical function.

The supplied materials do not establish whether a qualifying reconstruction-preserving method existed as of 1 November 2026; the umbrella review searched through 20 April 2026 and no additional freshness search was provided.
The specific animal local-delivery reduction-and-rebound assertion remains unverified rather than disproved.
The aseptic-revision comparator requires selection of a comparable endpoint, patient adjustment and statistical margin before it can serve as an interpretable benchmark.
No culture protocol or finite follow-up period alone can establish complete sterilization or lifetime freedom from recurrence.

The umbrella review’s supplementary materials and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review; its reported burden estimates remain limited by very low certainty and heterogeneous definitions and follow-up.

brief.title: Curing bone and implant infections while keeping them
possible: People with an infected joint replacement or bone-fixing implant could clear the infection while keeping the functioning implant. Treatment would end without antibiotics continuing indefinitely. The target is mature biofilm: an established community of bacteria attached to a surface.
The broader goal includes clearing longstanding bone infections while preserving structurally useful bone, including separated dead bone.
why: Patients could avoid operations to remove and replace a functioning implant because of infection. Keeping it could also reduce the bone lost during removal and reconstruction.

sources.who: Wouter Rottier, Jessica Seidelman and Marjan Wouthuyzen-Bakker
sources.showed: Their review explains how bacteria in mature biofilm tolerate antibiotics and cause relapse after treatment stops. Longstanding infections often require implant removal.
sources.quote: Even prolonged courses of antimicrobial therapy may not effectively eradicate microorganisms present in biofilm, and hence, infections involving biofilm are prone to relapses after withdrawal of antimicrobial therapy
sources.cited_for: Mature biofilm helps explain why antibiotics can fail to cure an infection around an implant.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a dependable cure for mature biofilm infection while keeping the entire functioning reconstruction.

sources.who: Jiamin Lu, Kai Zhang and Yongfa Xia
sources.showed: Their review of reviews reported treatment failure in 73.6% of late chronic infections treated with surgical cleaning, antibiotics and implant retention. This estimate had very low certainty.
sources.quote: The overall certainty of evidence was generally low.
sources.cited_for: Existing treatment has substantial failure rates in longstanding infections, although the estimates are uncertain.
sources.not_established: These pooled outcomes do not demonstrate reliable clearance of mature biofilm with the entire functioning reconstruction retained.

sources.showed: Hip replacement materials were associated with the risk of revision, surgery to replace an implant. Certain ceramic or zirconium heads paired with a specially treated plastic liner or cup had the lowest risk. The study was observational.
sources.quote:
Hip prostheses with a delta ceramic or oxidised zirconium head and highly crosslinked
polyethylene liner or cup had the lowest risk of revision throughout the 15 years follow-
ing surgery.
sources.cited_for: Implant materials affect long-term replacement risk, a separate question from curing an established infection.
sources.not_established: The study did not test whether mature biofilm infection could be cured while retaining an implant.

shown: Selected early infections can already be treated with surgical cleaning and antibiotics while keeping the implant. Antibiotics that act within biofilm also exist, with usefulness depending on the bacteria and clinical circumstances.

Lu and colleagues reported pooled infection clearance of 88% after surgery that retained a stable thigh-bone component of an infected hip replacement. Other components were replaced, so this preserved part of the reconstruction.
missing: A reproducible cure for mature biofilm infection that lasts after treatment ends, with the entire functioning reconstruction retained.
Treatment that reaches infected surfaces and surrounding bacterial reservoirs while preserving the implant, bone and soft tissue needed for function.
Evidence that infected bone, including separated dead bone, can remain mechanically useful after durable infection clearance.

milestones.label: Infection stays controlled after treatment ends
milestones.explanation: A planned patient study would have to show infection control for two years after finite treatment, with a functioning reconstruction retained and no indefinite antibiotics. This would test whether control lasts after treatment stops.

milestones.label: Agreed measures capture infection, function and harms
milestones.explanation: A study would have to define sampling, infection control, recurrence, new infection, further surgery, amputation, death, function and harms before starting. This would make success interpretable without treating negative cultures as proof.

milestones.label: Outcomes match comparable revision surgery without infection
milestones.explanation: Results would have to match a comparable outcome after replacement surgery without infection in the same joint, accounting for patient differences within a preset statistical margin. This would set a meaningful comparison.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm breadth and useful bone preservation
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm results across defined implant and patient groups, and separately test chronic bone infection with separated dead bone. This would establish scope, including bone survival or incorporation and function.

uncertain: It remains unclear when separated dead bone can safely remain and provide useful structural support after infection treatment.
The proposed follow-up duration and comparison with surgery without infection are criteria to be justified, rather than agreed standards.
Negative cultures and finite follow-up cannot prove that every bacterium is gone or that infection will never return.

page.title: Cure of chronic periprosthetic joint infection with implant retention
page.definition: A finite treatment course cures chronic infection around a hip or knee replacement while preserving every prosthetic component and weight-bearing joint function. The target is established biofilm, a surface-associated bacterial community; neither continuing antibiotics nor continuing phage treatment qualifies as cure.

goal.need: A 2026 umbrella review included 53 reviews of periprosthetic joint infection. Its pooled failure estimates for debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) have very low certainty and heterogeneous follow-up. Chronic biofilm infection often requires implant removal for source control. Removing well-fixed implants and excising surrounding bone can compromise joint function.

figures.caption: Pooled DAIR failure estimates in the 2026 umbrella review
rows: Late chronic hip or knee PJI
figures.note: Descriptive estimates with heterogeneous definitions and follow-up. Table 2 does not supply patient denominators for these estimates. Failure is not a measurement of microbiological sterilization.

statements.body: International Consensus Meeting on Musculoskeletal Infection, Hip and Knee workgroup
statements.quote: Success is typically viewed as long-term eradication of infection off antibiotics, but function must be maintained.

statements.body: Peptilogics, through chief executive Jonathan Steckbeck
statements.quote: We built PLG0206 from the ground up as the first drug to penetrate biofilm and eradicate the persister bacteria protected by it.
statements.context: The developer's stated design objective for investigational PLG0206, not a demonstrated clinical eradication result.

completion.title: A controlled study establishes two-year cure of chronic PJI with every prosthetic component retained.
completion.criterion: A prospective controlled study in a prespecified chronic periprosthetic joint infection population meets its published efficacy criterion for infection control off all infection-directed treatment, with every original prosthetic component retained and weight-bearing joint function preserved, at least two years after finite therapy ends. Successful patients are alive, no longer meet PJI diagnostic criteria, and neither undergo nor need further infection surgery. Chronicity follows the study's clinical definition; elapsed time alone does not establish mature biofilm. This establishes clinical cure rather than literal sterilization.
completion.set_by: Atlas; combined clinical completion criterion drawing on the ICM outcome categories and proposed minimum follow-up.
completion.basis: Searched ICM/MSIS recommendations, FDA clinical-evidence rules, and registered chronic-PJI and DAIR studies. No document set a combined test for chronic infection, every component retained, treatment cessation, function and a cohort-level efficacy threshold. ICM supplies the off-antibiotic outcome category and proposes two-year follow-up. The combined test is an Atlas criterion; its efficacy threshold must come from a published study protocol.

milestones.title: Treatment leaves no recoverable bacteria in an established biofilm assay.
milestones.criterion: Reach the minimum biofilm eradication concentration (MBEC): no surviving bacteria in the assay's recovery test after treatment of an established biofilm. This is an assay-specific endpoint, without a clinically validated susceptibility breakpoint. Related ex vivo evidence published on 24 November 2021 found culture-negative treated components from 10 of 17 chronically infected knee prostheses; the components had been removed, so this was not patient cure.
milestones.set_by: Biofilm MBEC convention, recognized in ICM 2025 Question B7 and operationally defined by Badha and colleagues. The cited explant result concerns knee replacements.
milestones.threshold_quote: associated with no surviving bacteria (no turbidity).

milestones.title: Treatment clears the retained implant and surrounding tissues in every treated animal.
milestones.criterion: Meet the published ideal preclinical target: complete infection eradication from the implant and surrounding tissues in all treated animals, with function restored. Infection must precede treatment. A rabbit study published on 16 September 2022 treated eight animals with PLG0206 plus antibiotics: 38% had culture-negative implants and 63% survived to 28 days. Treatment began two days after infection; these results do not establish eradication of chronic mature biofilm.
milestones.set_by: Moriarty and colleagues' international expert recommendations for orthopedic device-infection studies, published in 2019; an ideal eradication target, not a regulatory requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: complete eradication of infection in all test-treated animals

milestones.title: A patient with chronic PJI receives an investigational treatment under human-use authorization.
milestones.criterion: Administer an investigational treatment to at least one patient with chronic PJI under FDA expanded access: serious disease, no satisfactory alternative, inability to enter a trial, justified benefit–risk and no interference with development. A report published on 27 June 2026 describes one 96-year-old man with hip and knee PJI treated under IND 28197. He was asymptomatic off antibiotics at two years, but continued phage treatment and positive cultures establish suppression, not cure.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, published expanded-access eligibility criteria; authorized administration is the human-use milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: Potential patient benefit justifies the potential risks of treatment.

milestones.title: A retained-implant treatment reduces 12-month infection failure in a randomized trial.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate superiority to placebo plus DAIR on treatment failure at 12 months in a randomized, double-blind study. RETAIN specifies this test for PLG0206 in knee PJI, with approximately 240 participants planned; its first enrollment was announced on 10 March 2026. No comparative efficacy result was found. This protocol's endpoint does not by itself establish chronic-infection cure with every component retained.
milestones.set_by: Peptilogics, RETAIN protocol NCT07214311, described in its sponsor announcement and UK Health Research Authority summary; the published test concerns knee PJI.
milestones.threshold_quote: The study will test if rinsing the joint with PLG0206 works better than doing the procedure without it.

not_found: No controlled clinical result meeting the combined completion criterion was found.
No external completion threshold or qualifying clinical dataset was found for curing chronic osteomyelitis while preserving a sequestrum, a separated fragment of dead bone.
ClinicalTrials.gov records for NCT04787250, NCT05269121, NCT05269134 and NCT07214311 opened only as page shells.
A full RETAIN statistical analysis plan specifying its numerical superiority boundary was not found.

results.finding: Among 70 staphylococcal isolates from hip and knee infections, 54–87% were categorized as resistant by MBEC, depending on the antimicrobial.
results.detail: The cohort included 17 knee replacements, but assay results were not reported separately for knee-derived isolates. Resistance categories used clinical MIC breakpoints, not validated biofilm susceptibility breakpoints.
results.quote: For all antimicrobial agents, a greater proportion of the strains was categorized as resistant according to MBEC (54–87%) compared to MIC (0–51%).

results.finding: Chronically infected knee prostheses: 10 of 17 treated samples were culture negative.
results.detail: Removed components were treated ex vivo and sonicated before culture. Seven samples remained culture positive; the study did not determine an MBEC using a biofilm recovery assay.
results.quote:
Ten out of seventeen samples (59%) of the chronically infected prosthetics treated
ex vivo
with 1 mg/mL PLG0206 became culture negative.

results.finding: In a mouse knee infection model, 10/10 mice per group had culture-negative implants and tissues with three rifampin combinations.
results.detail: Treatment began two weeks after infection. Cultures were assessed one day after the six-week antibiotic course. Restoration of joint function was not reported, and the implant was a Kirschner wire.
results.quote:
All rifampin combination therapies resulted in
no CFUs detected from either the tissue homogenates or
implants.

results.finding: In a mouse knee PJI model, 0 of 10 implants per rifampin-combination group yielded bacterial growth after culture.
results.detail: Treatment began after two weeks allowed biofilm formation. This was an in vivo treatment followed by ex vivo recovery, not an MBEC assay; the study did not test antibiotic activity against biofilms in vitro.
results.quote:
All rifampin combination therapies resulted in
no CFUs detected from either the tissue homogenates or
implants.

results.finding: Among 79 prosthetic-joint C. acnes isolates, rifampin reached an MBEC90 of 2 mg/L.
results.detail: The cohort included 10 knee isolates. Results were pooled across joint sites, but eradication in at least 90% of the 79 isolates implies that at least one knee isolate reached the recovery-test endpoint. The assay used established biofilms on plastic, not retained implants.
results.quote: However, the minimal biofilm eradication concentration (MBEC) was high for all antimicrobial drugs tested (>32 mg/L), except for rifampin (2 mg/L).

results.finding: One patient with chronic knee PJI received bacteriophage therapy under FDA expanded access, IND 28197.
results.detail: The patient remained culture-positive and continued intermittent phage treatment; the reported outcome was suppression, not cure. The report does not individually document every expanded-access eligibility condition.
results.quote: Given limited treatment options, FDA-expanded access was obtained to start bacteriophage therapy.
